title: Nvidia opens Flora, the model suite it uses to label robot video
friendlyTitle: Nvidia has opened the models it uses to label robot video
summary: Nvidia's GEAR lab has released Flora, an open suite for the three labels a robotics model needs from video: when an action happens, how well each step went, and whether the episode succeeded. Nvidia says the same pipeline already labels 200,000 hours a day across 512 GB300 GPUs while training its GR00T models, and that it is roughly 125 times cheaper than calling GPT-6 Astra. The weights are on Hugging Face. On Nvidia's own table, Flora leads on human captioning and on catching failed steps, while Astra still leads on robot-video captions and on rubric scoring.
friendlySummary: Nvidia's robotics lab has released Flora, a set of open models for three labels a robot-training video needs: when an action happens, how well each step went, and whether the task succeeded. Nvidia says this pipeline already labels 200,000 hours a day on 512 of its GB300 chips while it trains its GR00T robot models. It also says Flora is about 125 times cheaper than asking GPT-6 Astra to do the same job. The weights are on Hugging Face. On Nvidia's own chart, Flora is better at human video and at spotting failed steps. Astra is still better at describing robot video and at scoring against a written rubric.
whyItMatters: If you are labelling robot or human demonstration video, the expensive part is no longer only the camera. A frontier model can write the captions, and the bill scales with the hours. Flora is Nvidia's argument that a smaller open suite can do that job in its own training loop. The scores are Nvidia's, and on robot video the frontier model still describes the action more precisely. Use the open weights to measure your own tapes, not to treat the 125-times figure as an invoice.
